# Digital Venture Studio

> Digital Venture Studio (DVS) helps solo founders and small teams make the decision most founders skip — whether an idea is worth building at all — and then build it. Writing by founder Rick Musial on the go/no-go decision, founder-market fit, venture validation, and the design choices that make tools worth trusting.

## Core

- [Digital Venture Studio — home](https://digitalventurestudio.com/): What DVS is, the method, products, and services.
- [Writing (blog index)](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/): All essays on the go/no-go decision and founder counterintuitions.

## Writing

- [They’re calling it spec-driven development. The spec was the point all along.](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-spec-was-the-point): GitHub shipped Spec Kit, AWS shipped Kiro, and Ethan Mollick called it “specs, not tricks” — the industry decided the specification, not the code, is the real artifact. That’s the premise Touchstone was built on from the start: every verdict ships a build-ready document suite, and the No-Go that keeps the spec honest.

- [The word on your proof matters more than the proof](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/word-on-your-proof): Proof doesn't travel — the word on it does. Why "Approved" beats "STATUS: GO 7.2" to everyone who wasn't in the room, and how to say the same true thing in the reader's language. The proof earns the claim; the word delivers it, and to anyone who wasn't in the room the word is the proof.
- [You can't QA your own values](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/you-cant-qa-your-own-values): You can test whether your product works, but not whether it says what you meant — that needs someone who isn't you. Your brain autocorrects to the version in your head, so your own typos (and your own meaning) survive every pass; the values version is the dangerous one. The surfaces that travel without you in the room, and the one outside-reader test that finds the gap.
- [The three signs your idea is a project, not a business](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/project-not-a-business): A project is worth doing; a business is something strangers keep paying for. Three signs you're building one and calling it the other — you're the only one who has to want it, the money is a someday not a mechanism, and it only improves when you add to it rather than when the market pulls.
- [Why most founders confuse enthusiasm with validation](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/enthusiasm-is-not-validation): Enthusiasm is a fact about you and the people who like you; validation is a fact about the market. They feel identical from the inside, and your own excitement always points up — so it's a reading you can't use. How to separate the two before you bet a year on the wrong one.
- [Scratch your own itch is dangerous advice](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/scratch-your-own-itch-is-dangerous-advice): Why "build something you need" is only half right, and the one question that separates an idiosyncratic itch (real for a market of one) from an early one (real but ahead of the market).
- [Founder-market fit is two different things](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/founder-market-fit-is-two-different-things): Founder-market fit is founder advantage AND problem validity — most founders only check one, and the gap is where ventures quietly die.
- [The founder-market fit problem nobody talks about](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-founder-market-fit-problem-nobody-talks-about): Validation tools score the idea; few ask whether you're built for what the market will cost you.
- [When the X-ray is perfect every time, the only thing that matters is bedside manner](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/when-the-x-ray-is-perfect-every-time): On AI tools, accuracy, and why trust is the differentiator once accuracy is commoditised.
- [The catastrophe you're trying to avoid](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-catastrophe-youre-trying-to-avoid): The real cost of skipping the go/no-go decision before you build.
- [The question you should answer before you write a single line of code](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-question-you-should-answer-before-you-write-a-single-line-of-code): The go/no-go decision, framed for first-time founders.
- [Admiration is unstable fuel](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/admiration-is-unstable-fuel): The founders who burn out aren't the ones nobody encouraged. They ran on admiration — and admiration is unstable fuel. Why conviction is the only thing that survives the silence.
- [The people who like your idea vs the people who'd miss it](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/who-would-miss-it): Likes are abundant and cheap. The signal that matters is rarer: who would actually feel the absence if your product vanished tomorrow? Build for the missers, not the likers.
- [Conviction isn't certainty](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/conviction-isnt-certainty): Conviction isn't the absence of doubt, and it isn't refusing to hear no. It's the reason that survives an honest no. How to tell conviction from its dangerous twin, stubbornness.
- [What to do when the admiration stops](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/when-the-admiration-stops): Every founder hits the quiet stretch where the applause dries up and it's just you and the work. Conviction isn't a feeling you wait for — it's something you build. Here's how.
- [You can't be your own second opinion](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/you-cant-be-your-own-second-opinion): You can now run a full VC-grade idea validation for free — six phases, ending in a go/no-go. It still won't tell you the truth about your idea, for one structural reason: you're the one holding the prompt.
- [Encouragement is not a second opinion](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/encouragement-is-not-a-second-opinion): The people who care about you — and the helpful AI — are compromised graders too. They optimise for your morale, not your clarity. What a real second opinion actually requires.
- [The feedback your idea can survive](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-feedback-you-can-survive): Asking for feedback can be a sophisticated form of avoidance. Founders unconsciously pick the people, questions, and framing that can't return a no — and call it research.
- [The No You Can't Give Yourself — free field guide](https://digitalventurestudio.com/the-no): A 36-page field guide on why a founder cannot be their own second opinion, and how to get a real verdict instead. Free; delivered by email.
- [Go looking for the no](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/go-looking-for-the-no): If you can't validate yourself, encouragement isn't a verdict, and you quietly pick the feedback your idea can survive — the move that's left is the uncomfortable one: go looking for the no.
- [The best product doesn't win](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-best-product-doesnt-win): You assume the better product wins. It doesn't — the most trusted one does. And trust is built the one way founders are most tempted to skip: being willing to say no.
- [The build-or-don't decision nobody actually makes](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-build-or-dont-decision): Most founders don't decide not to build — they just keep researching. The three things the build-or-don't decision actually needs, and why.
- [Will anyone actually pay? Most founders never really ask.](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/will-anyone-actually-pay): "Would this help someone?" and "will someone pay for this?" feel like the same question. The gap between them is where good ideas quietly die a year in.
- [The day your co-founder stopped being independent](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-day-your-co-founder-stopped-being-independent): Before you sign, a co-founder who knows your market is the cleanest outside read you'll get on your idea. The day you split the equity, that independence quietly expires — and almost nobody notices it go.
- [Your runway is grading your idea](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/your-runway-is-grading-your-idea): Ten signups reads as a start at eighteen months of runway and as traction at four. The evidence didn't change — the money did. How to stop your bank balance grading your idea.
- [You believe the evidence and still can't stop](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/you-believe-the-evidence-and-still-cant-stop): Stubbornness refuses the evidence. Conviction weighs it and holds. Sunk cost is a third thing — you accept the evidence completely, and the size of the bill won't let you act on it.

- [What your first sale actually proves](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/what-your-first-sale-actually-proves): One real sale beats a thousand signups — and it's still the most over-read data point in a venture. What a first sale proves, what it can't, and why its provenance decides everything.
- [The second gate opens after they pay](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/the-second-gate-opens-after-they-pay): Every honest founder post stops at the moment someone pays. The venture doesn't. There's a second gate past the first sale - quieter, recurring - and it's the one that decides whether you have a business.
- [Carrying a no you went looking for](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/carrying-a-no-you-went-looking-for): You did the hard thing and went looking for the no. This is about the part nobody warns you about - the few days you carry it before you act, when the people you'd normally tell are the ones who can't hold it.
- [You don't have a distribution problem yet](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/you-dont-have-a-distribution-problem-yet): A founder asked how to distribute a product with no audience - then admitted he was starting to wonder what the point of building it was. Those are two different questions, and the second one is the real one.
- [A healthy platform is the dangerous one](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/a-healthy-platform-is-the-dangerous-one): Checkout X died overnight at around €600k a month in recurring revenue. Shopify was in perfect health at the time – and that is the part founders get wrong about platform risk.
- [Marketing has no definition of done](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/marketing-has-no-definition-of-done): A founder shipped features on schedule for months and did no marketing at all. He wasn't short of time. He was short of a ticket.
- [Your best reader will never use your vocabulary](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/your-best-reader-will-never-use-your-vocabulary): One reader answered six of my posts in two weeks and never once used a word I'd written. He understood all six. That gap is worth more than any survey.
- [Everyone likes it and nobody is buying](https://digitalventurestudio.com/blog/everyone-likes-it-and-nobody-is-buying): Thirty-one posts, twenty-three verdicts, zero paying customers. My own numbers, and the two questions I should have asked before I called it a demand problem.

## Products

- [Touchstone](https://usetouchstone.ai): A structured go/no-go validation platform for early-stage ventures.
- [Eulogize This](https://www.eulogizethis.com): A comedic tool that writes a heartfelt eulogy for anything you choose to lay to rest — a dead iPhone, a failed side project, a lapsed gym membership.
